summary: This informational document presents how existing MPLS protection mechanisms, both local and end-to-end, apply to the MPLS Transport Profile in ring topologies. It proposes no new mechanisms or protocols and builds on the requirements in RFC 5654 and the survivability framework in RFC 6372.

plainLanguage.summary: When computers are connected in a circle and one link breaks, traffic can go the other way. This shows how existing tools do that.

questions: how does mpls-tp protect ring networks
how do sub-path maintenance entities work
can mpls-tp protect point-to-multipoint in rings
subtitle: Protecting traffic in ring-shaped networks using existing MPLS tools.

tldr.problem: Ring-shaped networks are common in transport systems, but protecting traffic when a link or node fails is challenging. Different strategies exist, each with trade-offs in complexity, bandwidth, and coverage.
tldr.mechanism: The document applies existing MPLS-TP linear protection mechanisms to ring topologies by configuring Sub-Path Maintenance Entities (SPMEs) that can redirect traffic around faults using either steering (ingress switching) or wrapping (local rerouting) approaches.
tldr.outcome: Steering provides simplicity and scalability while wrapping minimizes latency impact. Both can be implemented with existing protocols, meeting the requirements for ring protection in MPLS Transport Profile deployments.

today: RFC 6974 is an Informational document describing how existing MPLS-TP linear protection can be applied to ring topologies. It provides guidance for network operators deploying MPLS in ring-shaped transport networks. The document does not define new protocols, but rather explains how to apply existing mechanisms effectively in ring topologies.

sections.title: Ring Topologies and Protection
sections.content:
Ring topologies connect a series of network nodes in a circular arrangement, where each node connects to exactly two neighbors. Rings are common in transport networks because they are simple to design and operate. However, when a link or node fails, all traffic on that failed component is lost unless the network can quickly reroute to the other path around the ring.

The MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) standard defines requirements for protecting traffic in ring topologies. The document addresses two scenarios: protecting point-to-point paths that enter and exit the ring at single nodes, and protecting point-to-multipoint paths that branch to multiple egress nodes. It also addresses three types of faults: link failures, node failures, and operator commands that trigger protection actions.
sections.plainLanguage: A ring network is like a circle of people. If one person in the circle can't talk to their neighbor anymore, messages can still go around the other way. This document explains how to make that automatic in MPLS networks.

sections.title: Two Protection Strategies: Wrapping and Steering
sections.content:
Wrapping is a local protection mechanism. When one node detects a fault on an adjacent link or node, it immediately wraps traffic around the ring on an alternate path to reach the far side of the fault. The far-side node recognizes this wrapped traffic and wraps it back onto the normal path. Wrapping is fast because no notification delay is required, and each node makes independent local decisions. However, it uses double bandwidth on some links (traffic goes both directions) and requires operators to pre-configure whether they are protecting link failures or node failures.

Steering reroutes traffic at the ingress node. The ingress node detects a fault anywhere on the working path (using OAM messaging) and switches all traffic to the alternate path around the ring. Steering is simpler from a configuration perspective—operators do not need to choose between link and node protection in advance. However, there is a delay while the ingress node learns of the fault.
sections.plainLanguage: Wrapping is like people on both sides of a broken link immediately turning around to hand messages back the other way. Steering is when the sender gets told "that way is broken, send it the other way instead." Wrapping is faster but uses more effort. Steering is simpler but there is a delay in being told.

sections.title: Sub-Path Maintenance Entities for Protection
sections.content:
The MPLS-TP framework introduces Sub-Path Maintenance Entities (SPMEs), segments of a path that can be monitored and protected independently. An SPME is essentially a tunnel between two nodes that can carry multiple end-to-end paths inside it.

For ring protection, the document recommends configuring pairs of SPMEs: a working SPME carrying traffic in one direction and a protection SPME on the alternate route. Both SPMEs can be monitored continuously for faults. If the working SPME fails, traffic automatically switches to the protection SPME. For steering, the two SPMEs go from ingress to egress in opposite directions. For wrapping, segment-based SPMEs protect individual links or node-level SPMEs protect individual nodes. This approach allows aggregating protection of multiple end-to-end paths using a single pair of SPMEs.
sections.plainLanguage: An SPME is like a protected tunnel through the ring. Two parallel tunnels are configured: one for normal use and one as backup. When the normal tunnel breaks, the backup tunnel takes over. Multiple messages can share the same tunnels.

sections.title: Protecting Point-to-Multipoint Paths
sections.content:
Point-to-multipoint (P2MP) paths enter the ring at one node and exit at multiple nodes. For wrapping, the document describes an optimization called Ring Optimized Multipoint Wrapping (ROM-Wrapping). Rather than wrapping all the way around the ring, ROM-Wrapping configures protection paths that only go to the nodes beyond the failure point. This reduces the number of hops and bandwidth used compared to basic wrapping.

For steering with P2MP, the technique uses context labels defined in RFC 5331. Two unidirectional P2MP SPMEs are configured from the ingress node in opposite directions, with egress points at every node on the ring. Each egress node independently switches from the working to the protection SPME when it detects a fault. Context labels determine what each node does with the traffic at each SPME, allowing fine-grained control of where data exits the ring without requiring the ingress node to know the details.
sections.plainLanguage: When one sender needs to reach many receivers on a ring, protection is trickier. One smart approach wraps data only as far as it needs to go beyond the break. Another approach uses labels to tell each receiver which path to listen to, and they switch if one path breaks.

sections.title: Comparing Protection Approaches
sections.content:
The document analyzes the trade-offs between steering and wrapping for a ring with N nodes. Steering requires configuring O(2N²) SPMEs (two from each node to every other node) but requires only 3 OAM sessions per node and uses single bandwidth on each link. Wrapping requires only O(2N) SPMEs but needs multiple OAM sessions and uses double bandwidth on links near the failure.

For point-to-multipoint, ROM-Wrapping can partially recover from double failures while basic wrapping cannot. However, basic wrapping has a limitation: operators must choose in advance whether they are protecting against link or node failures. ROM-Wrapping does not have this limitation.

The document recommends steering for point-to-point ring protection due to its simplicity and scalability. It does not require pre-configuration of link versus node protection, scales well, and uses less bandwidth. Wrapping remains viable for specific scenarios such as P2MP distribution where ROM-Wrapping offers benefits.
sections.plainLanguage: Steering is simpler to set up and uses less bandwidth, but requires telling the sender about faults. Wrapping responds instantly but needs more bandwidth and complex setup. For most situations, steering is better.

sections.title: Coordination and Summary
sections.content:
Protection switching between endpoints must be coordinated, especially when unidirectional faults are detected or operator commands (such as Forced Switch) are used. The document notes that the Protection State Coordination Protocol specified in RFC 6378 provides all necessary coordination mechanisms for ring protection, whether using steering or wrapping.

RFC 6974 demonstrates that existing MPLS-TP linear protection mechanisms, combined with SPMEs, provide efficient solutions for ring topology protection. The mechanisms are not new protocols but applications of existing standards to the specific needs of rings. This approach aligns with the MPLS-TP design philosophy of reusing proven mechanisms rather than developing ring-specific protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: The endpoints of a protected path need to talk to each other about switching to the backup path, especially when things get complicated. There is already a standard protocol for this coordination. No new protocols are needed; just apply the existing ones to rings.
